# Introduction

hakobu runs your projects on servers you own. A project says what it needs in a file in its repository, `hakobu.toml`; CI builds each commit into images; the server pulls the new release and swaps it in with no downtime, then tells the commit how it went. There's no panel and no database: the file is the state, and the code that keeps your data safe (deploys, backups, secrets, alerts) is written and tested once, in hakobu.

## What it does

- **Deploys by pull.** CI pushes a release image; the server checks its tag every 30 seconds and deploys a new one. Nothing connects to the server from outside, and any CI that can push an image works. The commit gets a `hakobu/deploy` status, and the CI job waits for it, so a failed deploy is a red commit with the reason.
- **Safe deploys.** Before a deploy with migrations, hakobu dumps the databases; migrations run in the new image, and if they fail, the running version stays. The new version takes traffic only once it answers its health check. A deploy never deletes data: what the file no longer has is kept until a person deletes it.
- **Databases and caches.** PostgreSQL databases with their own users, and Valkey (Redis-compatible) caches, with passwords made on the server and handed to the apps as variables.
- **Secrets in the repository**, each sealed with [age](https://age-encryption.org) to the server and to you: anyone, an agent too, can add one; only the server and you can read them.
- **Backups** of every database and volume each day, sealed, to any S3 bucket and a copy elsewhere, each restored into scratch right after upload to prove it restores.
- **Alerts** by email when an app is down, a deploy or backup fails, the disk fills, or the audit finds a port open to the internet or a container hakobu didn't start; a pulse to a dead man's switch says hakobu itself is alive.
- **Agents welcome, nothing on your laptop.** Each server is its own MCP server, over SSH: your agent sees status and logs, deploys, rolls back and sets a repository up, with a skill for Claude Code that says how to change the file and migrations safely. You run the same commands, `ssh kasl-1 status`. Deleting or restoring data is root's, and the agent can't.

## What it needs

- A Linux server (Debian or Ubuntu, amd64 or arm64) with systemd, and SSH to it as root, once, to install. The installer sets up rootless Docker, and hakobu then updates itself.
- `ssh` on your laptop, which it has: you and your agent reach hakobu through it, with keys that run hakobu's commands and nothing else. hakobu's API listens on the server's loopback and nowhere else.
- A registry for the images (GitHub's ghcr.io works with no setup) and a CI to build them (the workflow hakobu provides is for GitHub Actions).
- For backups, an S3 bucket (Cloudflare R2, Hetzner Object Storage, AWS, any other); for alerts, an SMTP account.
- For the web, either ports 80 and 443 (hakobu gets Let's Encrypt certificates) or a Cloudflare Tunnel.

hakobu calls no provider's API: no DNS, no cloud, no Git host beyond the commit status. What's different in each project (its file, Dockerfile, migrations, DNS records) is for you or your agent to write.

Start with [a server](https://hakobu.dev/docs/install/index.md), then [a project](https://hakobu.dev/docs/project/index.md).

# A server

You need a new Debian or Ubuntu server you can SSH to as root (or a user with sudo), and nothing on your laptop but `ssh`. You, or your agent, run one line:

```bash
ssh root@203.0.113.7 'curl -fsSL https://hakobu.dev/install.sh | HAKOBU_NAME=kasl-1 HAKOBU_INGRESS=public HAKOBU_ACME_EMAIL=you@example.com bash'
```

That's the one time anything runs on the server by hand. It installs rootless Docker (as the user `hakobu-docker`), unattended upgrades, and hakobu (its signature checked) as a sandboxed systemd service running as `hakobu`; writes `/etc/hakobu/server.toml` and makes the server's key; and makes an SSH user, `deploy`, whose keys run hakobu's commands and nothing else. At its end it prints:

```
For your agent, once (Claude Code):
  claude mcp add --scope user kasl-1 -- ssh -T deploy@203.0.113.7 mcp
For you, in ~/.ssh/config:
  Host kasl-1
    HostName 203.0.113.7
    User deploy
then ssh kasl-1 status
```

The first line gives your agent the server's own MCP server, over SSH; the block lets you write `ssh kasl-1 status`, as these docs do. After that hakobu updates itself (see [Updates](https://hakobu.dev/docs/updates/index.md)), and you and your agent reach it only through those commands. Then take [your owner's key](#your-owners-key), and set up [a project](https://hakobu.dev/docs/project/index.md).

## The SSH user

`deploy` logs in with the keys root has (or `sudo`'s user), copied at the first install without their options; `HAKOBU_SSH_KEYS` gives others, one a line. Each key is `restrict`ed to one forced command, hakobu's: no shell, no files, no port forwarding, whatever the client asks for. Its home and keys are root's, so nothing running as it could add a key. `HAKOBU_SSH_USER` names it otherwise (the installer won't take over a `deploy` that's there already).

| | |
|---|---|
| `ssh kasl-1 status` | what runs, the last deploy, alerts, backups |
| `ssh kasl-1 deploys` | the last deploys, and why one failed |
| `ssh kasl-1 logs PROJECT/APP [--worker]` | an app's output |
| `ssh kasl-1 deploy PROJECT [--force]` | check for its release now; again with `--force` |
| `ssh kasl-1 rollback PROJECT` | back one release |
| `ssh kasl-1 backup`, `backups PROJECT` | back up now, list them |
| `ssh -t kasl-1 secret set PROJECT APP NAME` | seal a secret, typed unseen: see [Secrets](https://hakobu.dev/docs/secrets/index.md) |
| `ssh kasl-1 server get`, `server set …` | the server's settings: see [Server config](https://hakobu.dev/docs/servers/index.md) |
| `ssh kasl-1 server update [--to v1.5.0]` | update hakobu |
| `ssh kasl-1 mcp` | the MCP server, for an agent |

They ask hakobu's API on its Unix socket, `/run/hakobu-api/api.sock`, which only root and `deploy`'s group may open; the kernel tells hakobu who's on the other end, so no token is kept anywhere: root may do anything, `deploy` what an operator may. Restore, destroy and the backups' buckets are root's: `ssh root@kasl-1 hakobu restore …`.

To let another person or agent in, add their key as root to `/home/deploy/.ssh/authorized_keys`, with the same options as the line there.

## Your owner's key

Every secret and backup is sealed to your owner's key as well as to the server's, so you can open them if the server is gone. Without `HAKOBU_OWNER_KEY`, the installer makes one, and its secret half waits on the server, root's alone, for you to take it into your password manager, in your own terminal, not an agent's:

```bash
ssh -t root@kasl-1 hakobu server owner-key
```

It shows the key, and once you type `saved`, takes it off the server. Until then, the [audit](https://hakobu.dev/docs/alerts/index.md) reminds you. With [age](https://age-encryption.org) of your own, give the public half instead: `HAKOBU_OWNER_KEY=age1…` (`age-keygen` makes a pair).

## SSH itself

SSH is safe with keys alone. Many images take passwords too (Hetzner's Ubuntu does), and the installer warns if the server does; turn them off, as your key logs you in already:

```bash
ssh root@kasl-1 'echo "PasswordAuthentication no" > /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-keys-only.conf && systemctl reload ssh'
```

The audit expects SSH to listen.

## Options

The installer asks nothing: everything comes from the environment.

| Variable | |
|---|---|
| `HAKOBU_NAME` | the server's name: lowercase letters, digits and `-` |
| `HAKOBU_OWNER_KEY` | your age public key; without it, the server makes one (above) |
| `HAKOBU_SSH_USER` | the SSH user for hakobu's commands; default `deploy` |
| `HAKOBU_SSH_KEYS` | its keys, one a line; default root's, the first time |
| `HAKOBU_INGRESS` | `public`, `tunnel` or `none` (the default): see below |
| `HAKOBU_ACME_EMAIL` | Let's Encrypt's contact, for `public` |
| `CLOUDFLARE_TUNNEL_TOKEN` | the tunnel's token, for `tunnel` |
| `TS_AUTHKEY`, `TS_TAGS` | a Tailscale auth key and tags, for the API to listen on the tailnet as well (for hakobu on a laptop, below) |
| `HAKOBU_CONFIG_EXTRA` | a file whose TOML goes at the end of the config: releases, registries, backups, alerts (see [Server config](https://hakobu.dev/docs/servers/index.md)) |
| `HAKOBU_VERSION` | a release; default the newest |

Run it again to update by hand: the config, the keys and the data stay.

## How the web gets in

- **`public`**: hakobu answers ports 80 and 443 itself, with a Let's Encrypt certificate for each app's domain (and only those). Point each domain's DNS at the server.
- **`tunnel`**: cloudflared runs on the server with your tunnel's token and sends requests to hakobu on loopback; the server needs no open port. In Cloudflare, route each domain of the tunnel to `http://localhost:8080`.
- **`none`**: apps aren't served to the web; for a server of workers only, or while you set it up.

## Back up the server's key

`/var/lib/hakobu/key.age` opens the server's secrets and backups. Your own key does too, so losing the server's isn't fatal, but a copy off the server spares you re-sealing secrets on a new one.

## hakobu on a laptop

You don't need it, but the CLI from the [releases](https://github.com/hakobudev/hakobu/releases) does the same from a laptop, for several servers at once: every `ssh kasl-1 COMMAND` above is `hakobu COMMAND` there, and `hakobu mcp` serves them all to an agent. Install a server with it, and it remembers the server and its operator token:

```bash
hakobu server create kasl-1 --ssh root@203.0.113.7 --ingress public --email you@example.com
```

It reaches the API (on the server's 127.0.0.1:7070) through SSH, with a key it makes for a user, `hakobu-tunnel`, that may reach that port and nothing else; `--tailscale` (with `TS_AUTHKEY`) has the API listen on the tailnet instead. Your age key is asked for the first time and kept in `~/.config/hakobu/owner.pub`. The API's tokens: the **operator**'s, kept in `~/.config/hakobu/servers.toml`, looks, deploys, rolls back, backs up and updates; the **admin**'s, shown once for your password manager, also restores and deletes. A server installed otherwise doesn't show them: `hakobu server create` it from the start.

# A project

A project is a repository with a `hakobu.toml` at its root. With a [server](https://hakobu.dev/docs/install/index.md) and its MCP added to your agent, ask it to set the repository up for hakobu: its `init` tool registers the release image on the server and gives the files, which it writes, leaving any that's already there:

- **`hakobu.toml`**, the project and its server, with an app for the agent to fill in from the repository's Dockerfiles: hakobu builds each app from its own;
- **`hakobu.secrets.toml`**, empty, sealed to the server's key and yours;
- **`.github/workflows/hakobu.yml`**, which builds each push to the default branch and waits for its deploy;
- **`.claude/skills/hakobu/SKILL.md`**, a section in **`CLAUDE.md`** and **`.claude/settings.json`**: see [Agents](https://hakobu.dev/docs/agents/index.md).

The release image is `ghcr.io/OWNER/REPO`, the repository's.

## Then

1. **The file.** Each app gets its `domain`, a `health` path it answers once it's ready (`/up` by default), and the databases and caches it uses: see [hakobu.toml](https://hakobu.dev/docs/hakobu-toml/index.md). The `validate` tool checks it, as CI does.
2. **Secrets.** The server sets the commit's status with a [fine-grained token](https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new) with **Commit statuses: Read and write** on this repository alone. Make one, and seal it, in your own terminal:

   ```bash
   ssh -t kasl-1 secret set kasl hakobu status_token
   ```

   Your agent then adds it to `hakobu.secrets.toml`; your app's own secrets go the same way. See [Secrets](https://hakobu.dev/docs/secrets/index.md).
3. **Push.** CI builds the apps, pushes them and the release; within 30 seconds the server deploys it, and the job turns green once it's live. `ssh kasl-1 status` and the MCP tools show it.

   The first time, while the job waits, make the release image public: on GitHub, the package `REPO` (not `REPO-APP`), **Package settings → Change visibility → Public**. Everything in it is sealed to the server's key and yours, and the server polls it with no token; until then, `status` says the registry refused. The apps' images stay private: CI seals the job's own token in each release, and the server pulls them with it while the job waits for the deploy. The token dies with the job, so the server keeps none for ghcr.io.

   A private release works too, with a token for the server to read it: a classic token with `read:packages` alone, given with `ssh kasl-1 server set registry ghcr.io --username YOU` (the password typed, hidden). It reads every package of your account, so a public release is the safer one.

## An arm64 server

Images are built on CI's runner, for its architecture. For an arm64 server, set `runner: ubuntu-24.04-arm` in the workflow.

## Tests first

The workflow is a job like any other: put your tests in a job of their own and add `needs: [test]` to the deploy job.

## With hakobu on a laptop

`hakobu init --server kasl-1`, in the repository, writes the same files, with an app already for each directory (the root and one level down) that has a Dockerfile, or a stack it recognizes (Node, Python, Go, …), and `.mcp.json` for `hakobu mcp`; `hakobu secret set hakobu status_token` seals the token straight into the file.

# hakobu.toml

What a project's server runs, at the root of its repository. It's strict: an unknown key, a typo or a reference to nothing is an error, so a mistake stops the deploy instead of quietly turning something off. `hakobu validate` checks it, and CI runs it before each build.

```toml
project = "crm"
server = "kasl-1"

[apps.web]
domain = "crm.example.com"
release = "bin/rails db:migrate"
worker = "bin/jobs"
uses = ["main", "cache"]
volumes = { uploads = "/rails/storage" }
env = { RAILS_LOG_LEVEL = "info" }

[apps.admin]
path = "admin"
domain = "admin.crm.example.com"
uses = ["main"]

[databases.main]

[caches.cache]
memory = "128mb"
```

Names (the project's, apps', databases', caches', volumes') are lowercase letters, digits and `-`, starting with a letter, up to 31 characters.

## The project

| Key | |
|---|---|
| `project` | the project's name, unique on its server |
| `server` | the server it deploys to; any other server refuses the release |

One repository is one project.

## Apps: `[apps.NAME]`

An app is one image serving HTTP, and optionally a worker from the same image.

| Key | |
|---|---|
| `path` | its directory in the repository, default the root; the app is built from the `Dockerfile` there |
| `image` | a ready image to run instead, `evoapicloud/evolution-api:v2.3.7` say: nothing is built. It names a version; the build pins the digest that version names then, which the server runs until the file names another |
| `domain` | where it's served on the web; without one, only the project's other apps reach it. One project's on the server: another's deploy with it is refused |
| `health` | a path that answers 2xx once the app takes requests; default `/up`. A deploy goes live only once it does |
| `port` | the port it listens on; default the image's `EXPOSE`, else 8080. It's in `$PORT` too |
| `release` | a command run once per deploy in the new image before it takes traffic, for migrations: if it fails, the running version stays. See [Deploys](https://hakobu.dev/docs/deploys/index.md) |
| `worker` | the command of a background process from the same image |
| `memory` | its limit, `512mb` or `1gb`; at least `64mb` |
| `cpus` | its CPU limit, `0.5` or `2` |
| `volumes` | name → mount path. Survives deploys and is backed up |
| `env` | variables, plain values only: secrets go in [hakobu.secrets.toml](https://hakobu.dev/docs/secrets/index.md). A value may name one hakobu gives the app as `${NAME}`: see below |
| `uses` | the databases and caches it uses: a list, or a map of name → prefix |

The app must listen on all interfaces (not only 127.0.0.1). `release` and `worker` run with `/bin/sh -c` in its image, which therefore needs a shell.

Each app also gets `HAKOBU_REVISION`, the commit it was deployed from: what to give an error tracker as the release, for one. An app whose image a commit didn't change keeps running, with the commit it was deployed from.

### `uses`

A database gives the app `DATABASE_URL`, `POSTGRES_HOST`, `POSTGRES_PORT`, `POSTGRES_DB`, `POSTGRES_USER` and `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`; a cache `REDIS_URL`, `VALKEY_URL`, `REDIS_HOST`, `REDIS_PORT` and `REDIS_PASSWORD`. Two of a kind would set the same variables, so give one a prefix:

```toml
uses = { main = "", jobs = "JOBS" }   # JOBS_REDIS_URL, JOBS_REDIS_HOST, …
```

### One app to another

The project's apps reach each other by name: `http://web:8000` from another app of the project, or its worker, is web's live version, whichever that is during a deploy. The port is the one the app listens on. Nothing outside the project reaches it so.

### Variables from variables

A ready image often wants what hakobu gives under a name of its own. `${NAME}` in a value is a variable hakobu gives the app: one from `uses`, `PORT` or `HAKOBU_REVISION`.

```toml
[apps.wa]
image = "evoapicloud/evolution-api:v2.3.7"
uses = ["gateway"]
env = { DATABASE_CONNECTION_URI = "${DATABASE_URL}?schema=evolution" }
```

### Volumes

An app with volumes is stopped before its new version starts, so two versions never write the same files: a few seconds down on each deploy. The worker shares them.

## Databases: `[databases.NAME]`

A database and its own user on the server's PostgreSQL, which all its projects share; its version is the server's. It has no keys. See [Databases](https://hakobu.dev/docs/databases/index.md).

## Caches: `[caches.NAME]`

A Valkey server of the project's own, with its own password.

| Key | |
|---|---|
| `memory` | its memory, default `256mb`, at least `16mb` |

## What a change does

- **Adding** an app, database, cache or volume makes it on the next deploy.
- **Removing** one doesn't delete it: a database, cache or volume is kept, *orphaned*, and only `hakobu destroy` (a person's, as root on the server, after a last backup) deletes it.
- **Renaming** is removing and adding: the new one starts empty and the old one is orphaned. For a database, the deploy stops instead and says so: deploy the new one, move the data, then take the old one out.

# Secrets

An app's secrets live in its repository, in `hakobu.secrets.toml` next to `hakobu.toml`, each value sealed on its own with [age](https://age-encryption.org) to two keys: the server's and yours. Anyone with the repository can add or replace a secret, an agent too; only the server and you can read one. The file is committed like any other, and its diffs show which secret changed, never a value.

## Adding one

You type the value, in your own terminal; the server seals it, and your agent puts it in the file:

```bash
ssh -t kasl-1 secret set kasl web STRIPE_KEY    # PROJECT APP NAME; typed, hidden
```

The server keeps the sealed value for 7 days. The agent's MCP tool `pending_secrets` gives it, as `STRIPE_KEY = "age:…"` for `[apps.web]`; the agent writes it into `hakobu.secrets.toml` (replacing the one there), pushes, and clears it. The value never goes through the agent, nor its chat: it sees only what's sealed, which it can't open. From a password manager, without typing:

```bash
op read op://crm/stripe/key | ssh kasl-1 secret set kasl web STRIPE_KEY
```

The names are in the file; to remove one, the agent deletes its line. An app gets its secrets as variables. A secret can't have the name of one the file already sets (in `env`, from `uses`, `PORT` or `HAKOBU_REVISION`): the server refuses that release rather than guess which wins.

## hakobu's own

`APP` `hakobu` is for hakobu itself. `status_token` is the GitHub token that sets the commit's `hakobu/deploy` status: a [fine-grained token](https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new) with **Commit statuses: Read and write** on the repository alone. A release from a GitHub repository without it is refused, so a deploy is never silent.

## How they reach the server

CI puts the file, still sealed, in the release image; the server opens it with its key as it deploys. A [rollback](https://hakobu.dev/docs/deploys/index.md) takes the older image but today's secrets, so a rotated key stays rotated.

Database and cache passwords aren't secrets you keep: the server makes them.

## A new server

A new server has a new key, which can't open what was sealed to the old one. Put the old server's key back from your copy of `/var/lib/hakobu/key.age`, or start the file anew for the new server and set each secret again (the file names them).

## With hakobu on a laptop

```bash
hakobu secret init               # start the file, sealed to the server's key and yours
hakobu secret set web STRIPE_KEY # read from stdin (or typed, hidden): never an argument
hakobu secret list               # names only
hakobu secret unset web STRIPE_KEY
```

These seal straight into the file, with no server: `secret init` asks it for its public key once.

# Deploys and CI

Nothing pushes to a server. CI builds each commit into a **release image** and pushes it to a registry under a tag (`main`); the server checks that tag every 30 seconds and deploys each new one. CI needs no access to the server, and the server no inbound connection.

## The release image

`hakobu build`, which the workflow runs, builds each app of `hakobu.toml` from the Dockerfile in its directory, pushes it as `IMAGE-APP`, then pushes the release last: a tiny image whose labels carry `hakobu.toml`, the sealed `hakobu.secrets.toml`, each app's image pinned by digest, and the repository and commit it came from. The release goes last, so a server never sees one whose apps aren't pushed yet. Every app of a commit deploys together.

With a `hakobu.secrets.toml`, `hakobu.toml` goes in sealed to its keys, as does CI's own token for ghcr.io (the job's `GITHUB_TOKEN`): the release reads nothing but its repository, commit and images' names to anyone else, so it can be public. The server pulls the apps with the token while the job waits for the deploy; it dies with the job. A deploy that starts later (the server was down, say) can't pull: run the workflow again, or give the server [credentials](https://hakobu.dev/docs/servers/index.md) for the registry, which it then uses instead. A rollback to images the server still has needs none.

## A deploy

1. **Plan**: the file against what runs. A wrong file, a secret the server can't open or a renamed database stops here, before anything changes.
2. **A dump** of each database the app uses, if it has a `release` command.
3. **`release`** in the new image, with the app's variables. If it fails, the deploy stops and the running version goes on.
4. **The new version** starts, next to the old one, and must answer its `health` path with 2xx.
5. **Traffic switches** to it; the old version stops. No request is dropped (an app with volumes is the exception: it stops first, see [volumes](https://hakobu.dev/docs/hakobu-toml/index.md)).

A deploy never deletes data: databases, caches and volumes gone from the file are kept, orphaned.

## The commit status

The server sets the commit's `hakobu/deploy` status: pending as it starts, then success, or failure with the reason. The workflow's `hakobu wait` waits for it (15 minutes by default), so the CI job fails when the deploy does. Without the [status token](https://hakobu.dev/docs/secrets/index.md) the release is refused.

The failure email, `ssh kasl-1 deploys` and `ssh kasl-1 logs PROJECT/APP` (or the MCP tools) say more.

## Migrations

`release` runs while the old version still serves, and if anything after it fails, the old version goes on against the migrated database. So a migration must work with the code before it:

- add columns nullable or with a default, and tables, freely;
- rename or drop in two deploys: first stop using the column, then drop it;
- don't change a column's type in place: add another and backfill;
- long backfills belong in the worker, not `release` (it's stopped after 30 minutes).

## Rollback

```bash
ssh kasl-1 rollback crm
```

deploys the release before the current one, with today's secrets, and holds the current one back until a newer one comes. It doesn't undo migrations: the dump taken before the last deploy stays on the server, in `/var/lib/hakobu/snapshots`, and `hakobu restore` puts back a [backup](https://hakobu.dev/docs/backups/index.md). `hakobu deploy crm` checks for a release now instead of in 30 seconds; `--force` deploys the current one again.

## The workflow

The `init` tool (or `hakobu init`) gives `.github/workflows/hakobu.yml`, which calls `hakobudev/hakobu/.github/workflows/build.yml` with:

| Input | |
|---|---|
| `version` | the hakobu release to build with; the same as the workflow's ref |
| `image` | the release image, without its tag; default `ghcr.io/OWNER/REPO` |
| `tag` | the tag the server polls; default `main` |
| `runner` | the runner, whose architecture the images get; `ubuntu-24.04-arm` for an arm64 server |
| `wait` | how long to wait for the deploy; default `15m` |

For a registry other than ghcr.io, pass `registry-username` and `registry-password` as secrets. Releases run one at a time per repository, each waiting for its deploy.

Another CI works the same way: run `hakobu build --image IMAGE --tag main` where it can push, then `hakobu wait` (it reads GitHub's statuses, so it needs `GITHUB_TOKEN` and the commit).

# Databases

`[databases.NAME]` in [hakobu.toml](https://hakobu.dev/docs/hakobu-toml/index.md) is a PostgreSQL database with its own user, in the server's one PostgreSQL, which every project on the server shares. Only the apps that `use` it get its address and password; the password is made on the server.

```toml
[apps.web]
uses = ["main"]

[databases.main]
```

The app gets `DATABASE_URL` (`postgres://…`), `POSTGRES_HOST`, `POSTGRES_PORT`, `POSTGRES_DB`, `POSTGRES_USER` and `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`; with a prefix (`uses = { main = "APP" }`), `APP_DATABASE_URL` and so on.

## Its version

The PostgreSQL image is the one this hakobu release pins, for every project on the server: a database has no version of its own.

## Shared memory

PostgreSQL keeps the memory of parallel queries, hashes and sorts in `/dev/shm`, of which Docker gives a container 64 MB, too little for a large query (`could not resize shared memory segment … No space left on device`). hakobu gives PostgreSQL a quarter of the server's memory, up to 1 GB; it's memory only while a query uses it.

## Migrations

Run them as the app's `release` command, and keep them backward compatible: see [Deploys](https://hakobu.dev/docs/deploys/index.md). Before each deploy with a `release`, the databases the app uses are dumped on the server.

## Backups

Every database is backed up daily, sealed, checked by a restore into scratch, and kept 7 days plus 4 weeks: see [Backups and recovery](https://hakobu.dev/docs/backups/index.md).

## Deleting one

Removing it from the file keeps it, orphaned. `ssh -t root@kasl-1 hakobu destroy PROJECT/NAME` deletes it after a last backup, at a terminal, typing its name to confirm.

# Agents (Claude Code, MCP)

hakobu is built so an agent can do the work that's different in each project (the file, the Dockerfile, migrations, DNS) while the parts that guard your data stay in tested code it can't change.

## MCP

Each server has its own MCP server, run on the server itself over SSH: the installer prints the line that adds it to Claude Code, named after the server.

```bash
claude mcp add --scope user kasl-1 -- ssh -T deploy@203.0.113.7 mcp
```

For another client, add a local (stdio) server whose command is `ssh -T deploy@203.0.113.7 mcp`. Nothing of hakobu runs on your machine: it's your `ssh` and your key, which may run hakobu's commands on that server and nothing else. The server tells the agent the address it was reached at, so when it asks you to run something (a secret to type, say), it gives the line whole, `ssh -t deploy@203.0.113.7 secret set …`: nothing about the server goes in `CLAUDE.md`, and your own `~/.ssh/config` may call it what you like.

Its tools: `status`, `deploys`, `logs`, `backups`, `settings` (the server's releases, buckets, mail, updates; no secrets), `deploy`, `rollback`, `backup`, `update` (hakobu itself, to a newer signed release), `init` (set a repository up), `validate` (check `hakobu.toml` and `hakobu.secrets.toml` as the server will) and `pending_secrets` (the secrets you sealed, for it to add).

## The skill

`.claude/skills/hakobu/SKILL.md`, which the `init` tool gives, tells Claude Code how deploys work, how to write `hakobu.toml`, that migrations must work with the version before, how to add secrets without seeing them, and what not to do. A short section in `CLAUDE.md` points to it and says to read the servers through the MCP tools, never a shell or docker. Each `init` gives this hakobu's version of both, and leaves the rest of `CLAUDE.md` alone.

## What an agent can't do

- **Delete or replace data.** `hakobu destroy` and `hakobu restore` are root's on the server, and need a person at a terminal typing a confirmation: without a terminal they refuse. The MCP server has neither, and `.claude/settings.json` denies both to Claude Code as well. The backups' buckets are root's too.
- **Read a secret, or see one.** You type a secret in your own terminal (`ssh -t kasl-1 secret set …`); the agent gets it sealed, and can't open it. The skill tells it never to ask for one in the chat.
- **Get a shell.** Its key runs hakobu's commands on the server and nothing else, as an operator: look, deploy, roll back, back up, update, change the settings but the buckets, or remove a release image that deploys a project (another could take the project then).

The logs an agent reads are written by your apps, and text in them could try to steer it; what it can do through its key is bounded the same either way.

## With hakobu on a laptop

`hakobu init` writes the same files, and `.mcp.json` for `hakobu mcp`, which runs on the laptop and talks to every server it knows, with the operator token: the same tools, for all of them.

# Server config

A server's settings change through its API, from your terminal or your agent's: no one edits a file on the server.

```bash
ssh kasl-1 server get                          # what's set, never a password or key
ssh kasl-1 server set release ghcr.io/kasl/crm:main   # the init tool does this
ssh -t kasl-1 server set mail --host smtp.example.com --from hakobu@example.com --to you@example.com --username …
ssh kasl-1 server set pulse https://hc-ping.com/… https://hc-ping.com/…/fail
ssh kasl-1 server set updates --auto patch --at 04:00
ssh -t kasl-1 server set registry registry.example.com --username …   # ghcr.io needs none
```

The backups' buckets are root's, as a change of them could stop the backups, or send them elsewhere:

```bash
ssh -t root@kasl-1 hakobu server set backups --endpoint https://ACCOUNT.r2.cloudflarestorage.com --bucket kasl-backups --access-key …
ssh -t root@kasl-1 hakobu server set backups --copy hetzner --endpoint https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com --region fsn1 --bucket kasl-copy --access-key …
```

Passwords and keys never go in an argument: each is typed, hidden (hence `-t`), or comes from its variable on a laptop (`HAKOBU_SMTP_PASSWORD`, `HAKOBU_S3_SECRET_KEY`, `HAKOBU_REGISTRY_PASSWORD`). A change is proved before it's kept: the mail server sends you a mail, a bucket takes an object and gives it back (a copy only takes one, as its key may only write). hakobu then restarts itself into it, as soon as no deploy or backup runs, and the command waits for that.

hakobu keeps them in `settings.toml` in its data directory.

## server.toml

The server's own file, `/etc/hakobu/server.toml`, readable by hakobu alone, is what the installer wrote: its name, the API's address, your key and the tokens' hashes, and how the web gets in. The settings above may be set there too (then `sudo systemctl restart hakobu`), and what it sets wins: the API refuses to change it. Like `hakobu.toml`, it's strict: an unknown key stops hakobu from starting, and `journalctl -u hakobu` says why.

```toml
name = "kasl-1"
listen = "100.101.102.103:7070"
owner_key = "age1…"
operator_token_sha256 = "…"
admin_token_sha256 = "…"

releases = ["ghcr.io/kasl/crm:main", "ghcr.io/kasl/site:main"]

[registries."registry.example.com"]   # ghcr.io needs none
username = "kasl"
password = "…"

[ingress]
mode = "public"
email = "you@example.com"

[backups]
at = "03:00"
[backups.primary]
endpoint = "https://ACCOUNT.r2.cloudflarestorage.com"
region = "auto"
bucket = "kasl-backups"
access_key = "…"
secret_key = "…"
[[backups.copies]]
name = "hetzner"
endpoint = "https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com"
region = "fsn1"
bucket = "kasl-backups-copy"
access_key = "…"   # a key that can only write
secret_key = "…"

[alerts]
pulse_url = "https://hc-ping.com/…"
pulse_fail_url = "https://hc-ping.com/…/fail"
allow_ports = [22]
[alerts.smtp]
host = "smtp.example.com"
port = 465
username = "…"
password = "…"
from = "hakobu@example.com"
to = "you@example.com"
```

## Keys

| Key | |
|---|---|
| `name` | the server's name; a project's `server` must match it |
| `listen` | the API's address, on the tailnet or 127.0.0.1 (reached through SSH); any other address is refused |
| `socket` | the API's Unix socket, default `/run/hakobu-api/api.sock`: root may do anything there, the SSH user what an operator may |
| `data_dir` | default `/var/lib/hakobu`: the key, state, deploy history, dumps |
| `owner_key` | your age public key |
| `operator_token_sha256`, `admin_token_sha256` | the tokens' SHA-256 (`hakobu server token` makes a new pair) |
| `releases` | the release images to deploy, one a project, by tag |
| `poll_every` | how often to check them; default `30s` |
| `registries."HOST"` | `username` and `password` to pull from a registry; for ghcr.io, the token CI seals in each release does without (see [Deploys](https://hakobu.dev/docs/deploys/index.md)) |
| `ingress` | `mode` (`public` or `tunnel`), `email` (Let's Encrypt's contact), `listen` (for `tunnel`, on loopback; default `127.0.0.1:8080`) |
| `backups` | `at` (UTC, default `03:00`), `keep_daily` (7), `keep_weekly` (4), `primary` and `copies`: see [Backups](https://hakobu.dev/docs/backups/index.md) |
| `updates` | `auto`: the newer releases hakobu installs by itself, `patch` (the default: 1.2.x of the 1.2 running), `minor` (any 1.x) or `none`; `at` (UTC, default an hour after `backups.at`): see [Updates](https://hakobu.dev/docs/updates/index.md) |
| `alerts` | `smtp`, `pulse_url`, `pulse_fail_url`, `allow_ports`: see [Alerts](https://hakobu.dev/docs/alerts/index.md) |

A bucket has `endpoint`, `region`, `bucket`, `access_key`, `secret_key`, and `prefix` (default `hakobu/NAME/`); copies have a `name`.

## Reaching the API

The API listens on 127.0.0.1:7070, and on a Unix socket, `/run/hakobu-api/api.sock`, for root and the SSH user's group: `ssh kasl-1 …` and `ssh kasl-1 mcp` go through the socket (see [A server](https://hakobu.dev/docs/install/index.md)). The audit expects SSH to listen.

With a Tailscale key at install, the API listens on the server's tailnet address instead of 127.0.0.1, for hakobu on a laptop. In your tailnet's policy, let your own devices reach the server's tag on port 7070; nothing else needs to. The installer leaves Tailscale's SSH, routes and DNS off.

## From a laptop

```bash
hakobu server create kasl-1 --ssh root@203.0.113.7   # once: installs, and remembers it
hakobu server add kasl-2 http://100.101.102.103:7070  # one installed otherwise; the operator token on stdin
hakobu server list
hakobu status              # every server
hakobu --server kasl-1 deploys
hakobu server set mail kasl-1 --host …               # the commands above, with the server's name
```

The backups' buckets need the admin token there (`HAKOBU_ADMIN_TOKEN`, or typed).

# Backups and recovery

With a bucket in the [server's config](https://hakobu.dev/docs/servers/index.md), every database and volume on the server is backed up each day at `backups.at` (UTC). Caches aren't: they're caches.

## Each backup is

- **sealed** with [age](https://age-encryption.org) to the server's key and to yours, so the bucket alone reads nothing, and you can open a backup without the server;
- **copied**: written to the primary bucket and to each of `backups.copies`, another provider ideally, with a key that may only write, so a leaked key of the server can't delete the copies;
- **proved**: read back from the primary bucket and restored into scratch (a database counts its tables, a volume's archive is read through) before it counts as done;
- **rotated**: the newest of each of the last 7 days and one a week for 4 weeks are kept (`keep_daily`, `keep_weekly`); one made by hand counts as its day's. A bucket with object lock may refuse a deletion (a backup made by hand the day of another, under a 7-day lock); it's tried again on each rotation, and reported only if it's still refused a month on, a lock longer than the rotation keeps. The parts of a backup that never finished go a day later.

There's no catalog to lose: the backups are listed from the primary bucket itself.

A volume's app and worker are paused for the seconds the archive takes, so files that belong together (SQLite and its journal) are copied as of one moment.

A failed or unproved backup emails you (see [Alerts](https://hakobu.dev/docs/alerts/index.md)).

## Commands

```bash
ssh kasl-1 backup              # back up everything now
ssh kasl-1 backups crm         # list, newest first, with what reading each back found
```

## Restoring

```bash
ssh -t root@kasl-1 hakobu restore crm/main               # a database, from its newest backup
ssh -t root@kasl-1 hakobu restore crm/web/uploads --at 2026-10-20T03:00:12Z
```

A restore replaces the data, so it's root's, and needs a person at a terminal: an agent can't run it. (On a laptop, `hakobu restore` needs the admin token, from `HAKOBU_ADMIN_TOKEN` or typed, hidden.) The database or volume must exist on the server (deploy the project first).

## Before each deploy

A deploy with a `release` command first dumps the databases its app uses, on the server, in `/var/lib/hakobu/snapshots`: the state just before a migration, if it goes wrong.

# Alerts and audit

The server watches itself and emails you through any SMTP server (`[alerts.smtp]` in its [config](https://hakobu.dev/docs/servers/index.md)): one email when a problem starts and one when it's over, never a stream. Without SMTP, problems show only in `status`.

## What it watches

- an app that hasn't answered its health check for 3 minutes;
- a failed deploy (closed by the next one that works) or backup, and a backup that didn't prove it restores;
- the disk 85% full (closed under 80%);
- PostgreSQL not answering;
- an update of hakobu that didn't install (closed once it does), and a newer minor release of hakobu out for 14 days that this server hasn't updated to;
- the **audit**, hourly:
  - a port listening beyond loopback and the tailnet that isn't in `alerts.allow_ports` (80 and 443 are allowed for `public` ingress by themselves, and 22, as SSH is the way to hakobu);
  - a container hakobu didn't start;
  - unattended upgrades that haven't run for 3 days;
  - your owner's key still on the server, where the installer made it (`ssh -t root@SERVER hakobu server owner-key` takes it).

What's fixed closes by itself. Problems survive a restart of hakobu, so you aren't mailed twice.

The audit sees what listens on the machine, not a firewall in front of it (a cloud firewall is outside its view), and only TCP.

## The pulse

Every 15 minutes hakobu fetches `alerts.pulse_url`, or `alerts.pulse_fail_url` while a problem is open. Point them at a dead man's switch ([healthchecks.io](https://healthchecks.io) and the like): it emails you when the pulses stop, which is how you hear that hakobu, or the whole server, is down.

## Your apps' errors

hakobu doesn't collect errors or traces. Give an app a `SENTRY_DSN` [secret](https://hakobu.dev/docs/secrets/index.md) and any Sentry-compatible service has them.

# Updates

Each server looks for a newer hakobu once a day, and `status` (and the MCP `status`) shows one that's out. To update:

```bash
ssh kasl-1 server update               # the latest release
ssh kasl-1 server update --to v1.5.0
```

It waits and says how it went. An agent does the same with the MCP tool `update`: an update installs only a newer release signed by hakobu's key, so the most it can do is move a server forward. On a laptop, `hakobu server update [NAME]`, every server without one.

On the server, the API only asks: hakobu runs as a user that can't write its own binary, so it creates `update-request` in its data directory, and systemd (`hakobu-update.path`) runs the update as root. That checks the release's signature and checksum, refuses one that isn't newer, and runs the new release's own installer (the `install.sh` it carries), so an update does what installing it by hand does. If the new version doesn't come up within three minutes, the binary from before goes back in and is started again. `/opt/hakobu/update-status.json` says how the last update went, and status shows a failed one.

As root, `ssh root@kasl-1 hakobu server update [--to v1.5.0]` does the same without the API.

## By itself

Fixes install themselves: at `updates.at` (UTC, an hour after the backups by default) a server installs the latest release if it's a patch of the version it runs (1.2.3 → 1.2.4), and not during a deploy or the backups (it waits for the next day then). A release that didn't install isn't tried again by itself. Newer minor and major releases wait for `server update`; one that's been out for 14 days mails you.

```toml
[updates]
auto = "patch"   # or "minor" (any 1.x), or "none"
at = "04:00"
```

A server on v1.2.0 or older has no updater yet, and one on v1.4 or older no SSH user: run the installer on it once, which sets both up.

```bash
ssh root@kasl-1 'curl -fsSL https://hakobu.dev/install.sh | bash'
```

The config, the key and the data stay. Apps keep running; their proxies live in hakobu, so they don't answer for about half a second while it restarts. Docker is restarted only if its settings changed.

A server's MCP is always its own version. hakobu on a laptop is the binary from the [release](https://github.com/hakobudev/hakobu/releases). A project's workflow names its version (`version:` and the ref of `uses:`): bump both together, after its server is on that version or newer, as a release built by a newer hakobu may need it (from v1.4.0, `hakobu.toml` is sealed in the release).

## Signed releases

Releases are signed with an Ed25519 key that never leaves the release workflow. The installer and the workflow install a release only if its signature over `hakobu <version>` and its checksums is by that key, so neither a tampered download nor an older release under a newer name gets in.

# Security

What hakobu does to keep your apps and data yours, and what it doesn't promise.

## Nothing comes in

The server pulls its releases; no CI or panel connects to it. You and your agent reach it over SSH alone, with keys that run hakobu's commands and nothing else (no shell, no files, no forwarding); hakobu's API listens on loopback and a Unix socket, or on the tailnet, and nowhere else (any other address is refused); hakobu's own releases are signed, and install only if newer, and the web reaches apps only through 80/443 for their own domains, or a Cloudflare Tunnel with no port open at all. The [audit](https://hakobu.dev/docs/alerts/index.md) emails you about any other port that listens.

## Who may do what

On the API's socket the kernel says who connects: root may do anything, the SSH user (`deploy`, your agent's and yours) what an operator may: look, deploy, roll back, back up, update hakobu, change the settings but the backups' buckets. No token is kept for either. Restore and destroy are root's, need a person at a terminal typing a confirmation, and delete only what the file no longer has, after a last backup.

For hakobu on a laptop, the API's tokens do the same over TCP: the **operator** token, and the **admin** token, which alone restores or deletes; the server keeps only their SHA-256.

SSH is as safe as its keys: turn passwords off (the installer warns while they're on), and guard your key as you would the server.

## Isolation

hakobu runs as the unprivileged `hakobu` user, in a sandboxed systemd unit, and [rootless Docker](https://docs.docker.com/engine/security/rootless/) as another, `hakobu-docker`: neither a break-in into hakobu nor a container escape gets root, and an escape can't read hakobu's data. Containers run with `no-new-privileges` and without raw sockets. Each project has its own Docker network; each database its own PostgreSQL user, and each cache its own server and password.

## Secrets and backups

Sealed with age to the server's key and yours: see [Secrets](https://hakobu.dev/docs/secrets/index.md) and [Backups](https://hakobu.dev/docs/backups/index.md). The repository, the registry and the backup buckets hold nothing readable without one of the two keys. Backup copies go with a key that may only write.

## What's beyond it

The release image is trusted as it comes: whoever can push to its tag deploys to the server. A public release shows its repository, its commits and its apps' image names; the rest is sealed. Guard the registry, and CI's ability to push, as you would SSH. A malicious app can read its own secrets and its own databases, as any app can. A release names its project, and only the release image that first deployed a project may deploy it again, so one repository's CI can't take another project, and its databases; removing that image from the server needs the admin token.

## Releases

Signed, and installed only after checking the signature: see [Updates](https://hakobu.dev/docs/updates/index.md).

## Reporting a problem

Found a vulnerability? Please report it privately through [GitHub's security advisories](https://github.com/hakobudev/hakobu/security/advisories/new) rather than in an issue.

# Development

hakobu is open source under the MIT license: [github.com/hakobudev/hakobu](https://github.com/hakobudev/hakobu).

## Building

```bash
go build -o hakobu .
```

Requires Go 1.27+. The server side needs Linux, systemd and Docker; `install.sh` with `HAKOBU_BINARY=./hakobu` installs a local build on a test machine.

## Tests

`just check` runs what CI runs: build, vet, tests, govulncheck and golangci-lint. Tests that need Docker (they start their own containers: PostgreSQL, Valkey, an S3 server) run with `HAKOBU_DOCKER_TEST=1 go test ./internal/apply ./internal/backups`.

## These docs

The pages of hakobu.dev/docs are made from `docs/*.md` (the menu is `docs/nav.md`) by `go run ./tools/docsgen` into `site/docs/`; a test fails when they're behind the Markdown.

## Releases

Pushing a `vX.Y.Z` tag builds and publishes a release (`.github/workflows/release.yml`), signed with the key in the `HAKOBU_SIGNING_KEY` secret of the `release` environment; without it the release fails rather than going out unsigned. `just release-check` builds a snapshot without signing.

## Layout

- `main.go`, `internal/cli/`: the command line, the MCP server, and `hakobu ssh`, the SSH user's forced command
- `internal/spec/`: hakobu.toml
- `internal/seal/`: hakobu.secrets.toml
- `internal/server/`: the daemon: config, API (TCP and its Unix socket), polling, monitoring
- `internal/apply/`: plans and deploys a release; watches the release images
- `internal/ci/`, `internal/scaffold/`: `hakobu build`/`wait`, `hakobu init` and the skill
- `internal/backups/`: sealed backups to S3, their proof and rotation
- `internal/alert/`, `internal/audit/`: email, pulse, the audit
- `internal/ingress/`: 80/443 with Let's Encrypt, or the tunnel's loopback
- `internal/node/`, `internal/deploy/`, `internal/proxy/`: Docker on the server, each app's proxy
- `internal/registry/`, `internal/status/`: the registry client, the commit status
